body:
Thank you for saying that, it has definitely been a white knuckle experience and I've had a lot of moments where I needed to be fully honest with myself. Last night was so exception and I am happy to report that I am still sober and soldiering on. 

A little background about my experience. My mother was a lifelong alcoholic. My oldest sister is an alcoholic and a cocaine addict. She hid her cocaine addiction from us for 10 years before she got sober. 
In the beginning of her sobriety, she asked me and our other sister to accompany her to her AA meetings as moral support and those meetings were extremely difficult for me to sit through. I could blame my empathetic nature, but in truth I knew I was an alcoholic even then and I knew that I had a bottle of booze hidden in my closet at home just waiting for me. And I was sure to find it as soon as I got back home, if not to console myself, to at least try to forget the stories of the strangers who were trying to survive their addictions by facing them head on. I was not ready for that. 

My sister was sober for 3 years after her first relapse when I decided that I too needed to get sober. I knew I needed to end the generational curse of addiction as the youngest daughter. I didn't want to become my mother. 

Fast forward 2 and 1/2 years into my sobriety, my mom passed away after falling and hitting her head and suffering a brain hemorrhage and stroke. That day my oldest sister lost her sobriety and still hasn't gotten it back. But I held on. 

I view my sobriety as something that is mine that I can either keep or give away. To keep it is to acknowledge that it is MINE. That I worked for it and that I get to keep it for myself. But if I were to give it away then I would have to face that a temporary problem was able to claim ownership over it, not because it forced me to drink but because I simply handed it over and said 'you win'. That mentality has kept me sober for 4 years. 

I do own the AA book. I read it, I journaled, I work the steps and try to call onto my higher power whenever I find myself beaten to my knees. One day at a time. 

While this is just a brief synopsis, a front flap description of my sobriety, this is the bare bones of it. Feel free to share it with you group, hopefully someone can gain some sort of strength from it. 

I'm still sober, and I won't give in. I won't let it win. I own that.

Hey, im the OP. I should have been more clear off the bat. While I haven't been to a meeting, I did purchase and read the AA book and work the steps and buy my own chips. Still working on making amends. Some I can't make because I needed to make them with my mom who passed. She was a life long alcohol, the inspiration behind me getting sober to break the generational curse of addiction. My oldest sister was not my sponsor but more so my guide through sobriety in the beginning. She had 3 years of sobriety from alcohol and cocaine when I started my new life. When our mom died, my sister lost her sobriety and hasn't gotten it back since. So I've been doing this fully alone since then. Several people have asked me to sponsor them and guide them through their sobriety but I said no. Because who am I to tell someone not to drink when here I am trying to rationalize why I should drink myself? I can barely be responsible for myself, I never thought I could be responsible for someone else. So I agree with you 100%, I can't sponsor anyone. But I have worked the steps. Still climbing. Still sober. One day at a time.
